units.text: ⟦0⟧3.7 Problematic Regular Expressions⟦1⟧
units.sourceHTML: 3.7 Problematic Regular Expressions

units.text: Some strings are ⟦0⟧invalid regular expressions⟦1⟧ and cause ⟦2⟧ to issue a diagnostic and fail. For example, ‘⟦3⟧’ is invalid because there is no parenthesized subexpression for the back-reference ‘⟦4⟧’ to refer to.
units.sourceHTML: Some strings are invalid regular expressions and cause grep to issue a diagnostic and fail. For example, ‘xy\1’ is invalid because there is no parenthesized subexpression for the back-reference ‘\1’ to refer to.

units.text: Also, some regular expressions have ⟦0⟧unspecified behavior⟦1⟧ and should be avoided even if ⟦2⟧ does not currently diagnose them. For example, ‘⟦3⟧’ has unspecified behavior because ‘⟦4⟧’ is not a special character and ‘⟦5⟧’ is not a special backslash expression (see ⟦6⟧Special Backslash Expressions⟦7⟧). Unspecified behavior can be particularly problematic because the set of matched strings might be only partially specified, or not be specified at all, or the expression might even be invalid.
units.sourceHTML: Also, some regular expressions have unspecified behavior and should be avoided even if grep does not currently diagnose them. For example, ‘xy\0’ has unspecified behavior because ‘0’ is not a special character and ‘\0’ is not a special backslash expression (see Special Backslash Expressions). Unspecified behavior can be particularly problematic because the set of matched strings might be only partially specified, or not be specified at all, or the expression might even be invalid.

units.text: The following regular expression constructs are invalid on all platforms conforming to POSIX, so portable scripts can assume that ⟦0⟧ rejects these constructs:
units.sourceHTML: The following regular expression constructs are invalid on all platforms conforming to POSIX, so portable scripts can assume that grep rejects these constructs:

units.text: A basic regular expression containing a back-reference ‘⟦0⟧’ preceded by fewer than ⟦1⟧ closing parentheses. For example, ‘⟦2⟧’ is invalid.
units.sourceHTML: • A basic regular expression containing a back-reference ‘\n’ preceded by fewer than n closing parentheses. For example, ‘\(a\)\2’ is invalid.

units.text: A bracket expression containing ‘⟦0⟧’ that does not start a character class; and similarly for ‘⟦1⟧’ and ‘⟦2⟧’. For example, ‘⟦3⟧’ and ‘⟦4⟧’ are invalid.
units.sourceHTML: • A bracket expression containing ‘[:’ that does not start a character class; and similarly for ‘[=’ and ‘[.’. For example, ‘[a[:b]’ and ‘[a[:ouch:]b]’ are invalid.

units.text: GNU ⟦0⟧ treats the following constructs as invalid. However, other ⟦1⟧ implementations might allow them, so portable scripts should not rely on their being invalid:
units.sourceHTML: GNU grep treats the following constructs as invalid. However, other grep implementations might allow them, so portable scripts should not rely on their being invalid:

units.text: Unescaped ‘⟦0⟧’ at the end of a regular expression.
units.sourceHTML: • Unescaped ‘\’ at the end of a regular expression.

units.text: Unescaped ‘⟦0⟧’ that does not start a bracket expression.
units.sourceHTML: • Unescaped ‘[’ that does not start a bracket expression.

units.text: A ‘⟦0⟧’ in a basic regular expression that does not start an interval expression.
units.sourceHTML: • A ‘\{’ in a basic regular expression that does not start an interval expression.

units.text: A basic regular expression with unbalanced ‘⟦0⟧’ or ‘⟦1⟧’, or an extended regular expression with unbalanced ‘⟦2⟧’.
units.sourceHTML: • A basic regular expression with unbalanced ‘\(’ or ‘\)’, or an extended regular expression with unbalanced ‘(’.

units.text: In the POSIX locale, a range expression like ‘⟦0⟧’ that represents zero elements. A non-GNU ⟦1⟧ might treat it as a valid range that never matches.
units.sourceHTML: • In the POSIX locale, a range expression like ‘z-a’ that represents zero elements. A non-GNU grep might treat it as a valid range that never matches.

units.text: An interval expression with a repetition count greater than 32767. (The portable POSIX limit is 255, and even interval expressions with smaller counts can be impractically slow on all known implementations.)
units.sourceHTML: • An interval expression with a repetition count greater than 32767. (The portable POSIX limit is 255, and even interval expressions with smaller counts can be impractically slow on all known implementations.)

units.text: A bracket expression that contains at least three elements, the first and last of which are both ‘⟦0⟧’, or both ‘⟦1⟧’, or both ‘⟦2⟧’. For example, a non-GNU ⟦3⟧ might treat ‘⟦4⟧’ like ‘⟦5⟧’, or like ‘⟦6⟧’.
units.sourceHTML: • A bracket expression that contains at least three elements, the first and last of which are both ‘:’, or both ‘.’, or both ‘=’. For example, a non-GNU grep might treat ‘[:alpha:]’ like ‘[[:alpha:]]’, or like ‘[:ahlp]’.

units.text: The following constructs have well-defined behavior in GNU ⟦0⟧. However, they have unspecified behavior elsewhere, so portable scripts should avoid them:
units.sourceHTML: The following constructs have well-defined behavior in GNU grep. However, they have unspecified behavior elsewhere, so portable scripts should avoid them:

units.text: Special backslash expressions like ‘⟦0⟧’, ‘⟦1⟧’, and ‘⟦2⟧’. See ⟦3⟧Special Backslash Expressions⟦4⟧.
units.sourceHTML: • Special backslash expressions like ‘\b’, ‘\<’, and ‘\]’. See Special Backslash Expressions.

units.text: A basic regular expression that uses ‘⟦0⟧’, ‘⟦1⟧’, or ‘⟦2⟧’.
units.sourceHTML: • A basic regular expression that uses ‘\?’, ‘\+’, or ‘\|’.

units.text: An extended regular expression that uses back-references.
units.sourceHTML: • An extended regular expression that uses back-references.

units.text: An empty regular expression, subexpression, or alternative. For example, ‘⟦0⟧’ is not portable; a portable equivalent is ‘⟦1⟧’.
units.sourceHTML: • An empty regular expression, subexpression, or alternative. For example, ‘(a|bc|)’ is not portable; a portable equivalent is ‘(a|bc)?’.

units.text: In a basic regular expression, an anchoring ‘⟦0⟧’ that appears directly after ‘⟦1⟧’, or an anchoring ‘⟦2⟧’ that appears directly before ‘⟦3⟧’.
units.sourceHTML: • In a basic regular expression, an anchoring ‘^’ that appears directly after ‘\(’, or an anchoring ‘$’ that appears directly before ‘\)’.

units.text: In a basic regular expression, a repetition operator that directly follows another repetition operator.
units.sourceHTML: • In a basic regular expression, a repetition operator that directly follows another repetition operator.

units.text: In an extended regular expression, unescaped ‘⟦0⟧’ that does not begin a valid interval expression. GNU ⟦1⟧ treats the ‘⟦2⟧’ as an ordinary character.
units.sourceHTML: • In an extended regular expression, unescaped ‘{’ that does not begin a valid interval expression. GNU grep treats the ‘{’ as an ordinary character.

units.text: A null character or an encoding error in either pattern or input data. See ⟦0⟧Character Encoding⟦1⟧.
units.sourceHTML: • A null character or an encoding error in either pattern or input data. See Character Encoding.

units.text: An input file that ends in a non-newline character, where GNU ⟦0⟧ silently supplies a newline.
units.sourceHTML: • An input file that ends in a non-newline character, where GNU grep silently supplies a newline.

units.text: The following constructs have unspecified behavior, in both GNU and other ⟦0⟧ implementations. Scripts should avoid them whenever possible.
units.sourceHTML: The following constructs have unspecified behavior, in both GNU and other grep implementations. Scripts should avoid them whenever possible.

units.text: A backslash escaping an ordinary character, unless it is a back-reference like ‘⟦0⟧’ or a special backslash expression like ‘⟦1⟧’ or ‘⟦2⟧’. See ⟦3⟧Special Backslash Expressions⟦4⟧. For example, ‘⟦5⟧’ has unspecified behavior now, and a future version of ⟦6⟧ might specify ‘⟦7⟧’ to have a new behavior.
units.sourceHTML: • A backslash escaping an ordinary character, unless it is a back-reference like ‘\1’ or a special backslash expression like ‘\<’ or ‘\b’. See Special Backslash Expressions. For example, ‘\x’ has unspecified behavior now, and a future version of grep might specify ‘\x’ to have a new behavior.

units.text: A repetition operator that appears directly after an anchor, or at the start of a complete regular expression, parenthesized subexpression, or alternative. For example, ‘⟦0⟧’ has unspecified behavior, whereas ‘⟦1⟧’ is portable.
units.sourceHTML: • A repetition operator that appears directly after an anchor, or at the start of a complete regular expression, parenthesized subexpression, or alternative. For example, ‘+|^*(+a|?-b)’ has unspecified behavior, whereas ‘\+|^\*(\+a|\?-b)’ is portable.

units.text: A range expression outside the POSIX locale. For example, in some locales ‘⟦0⟧’ might match some characters that are not lowercase letters, or might not match some lowercase letters, or might be invalid. With GNU ⟦1⟧ it is not documented whether these range expressions use native code points, or use the collation sequence specified by the ⟦2⟧ category, or use the collation ordering used by ⟦3⟧ and ⟦4⟧, or have some other interpretation. Outside the POSIX locale, it is portable to use ‘⟦5⟧’ to match a lower-case letter, or ‘⟦6⟧’ to match an ASCII lower-case letter.
units.sourceHTML: • A range expression outside the POSIX locale. For example, in some locales ‘[a-z]’ might match some characters that are not lowercase letters, or might not match some lowercase letters, or might be invalid. With GNU grep it is not documented whether these range expressions use native code points, or use the collation sequence specified by the LC_COLLATE category, or use the collation ordering used by sort and strcoll, or have some other interpretation. Outside the POSIX locale, it is portable to use ‘[[:lower:]]’ to match a lower-case letter, or ‘[abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz]’ to match an ASCII lower-case letter.
